html:
Michael Commons’s Model of Hierarchical Complexity (MHC) treats development not as changes in "mental structures" but as the growth of one’s capacity to coordinate tasks that are themselves layered in ever-deeper recursive hierarchies. A given task is more complex when it organizes lower-order actions into a new, integrated whole, much as multiplication coordinates repeated addition. A performer’s stage is simply the order of the most complex task they can execute correctly (which separates "performance" from "task demand"), so the model applies equally to toddlers, corporations, or artificial agents. Commons and colleagues now distinguish 17 orders (numbered 0-16), but the logic is the same: each step demands qualitatively new syntheses of the step below. Higher-order organization isn’t just "doing more steps" or "putting steps in some remembered sequence". Commons draws a contrast between iteration (repeat the same action), mixtures (do some adds and some multiplies), and chains (a sequence, but the order could be permuted without being logically forced). Those don’t create a new order. New-order behavior is when the higher-order action uniquely and necessarily constrains how lower-order actions must be coordinated to satisfy the task (e.g., the distributive act forces a particular coordination of addition and multiplication, rather than any old chain of them). In other words, higher-order tasks operate on lower-order tasks in a way that involves structure-preserving, constraint-driven coordination (the relations) are doing real work), not "a list of subtasks."

Stages

Orders 0-3 - Pre-conceptual action.

Calculatory (0): programs that execute fixed computations with no generalization.

Automatic (1): "hard-wired" actions; single responses to a single stimulus.

Sensory-&-Motor (2): rote discrimination or movement without chaining (e.g., a limb withdrawal).

Circular Sensory-Motor (3): repetitive loops (grabbing, shaking, babbling) open-ended but not yet conceptual

Orders 4-9 - Language, logic, and concrete operations.

Sensory-Motor Conceptual (4): genuine concepts (morphemes, object categories) coordinate earlier loops.

Nominal (5): relations among concepts; single-word commands or labels.

Sentential (6): short sequential chains (phrases, simple scripts).

Preoperational (7): rudimentary deduction and stories; can follow lists of steps.

Primary (8): time-ordered empirical rules; simple arithmetic.

Concrete (9): full arithmetic, perspective-taking, deals and cliques (Piaget’s concrete operations writ large)

Orders 10-11 - Abstract and Formal thought.

Abstract (10): variables, quantifiers ("all," "none"); stereotypes and categories detached from instances.

Formal (11): linear causal arguments, single-unknown algebra, hypothesis testing (Piaget’s formal operations).

Post-formal orders 12-16 - Systems, metasystems, and beyond.

Systematic (12): coordinates multiple variables simultaneously; builds multivariate systems (economic, legal).

Metasystematic (13): compares and composes whole systems into metasystems, naming their properties (isomorphism, consistency); understanding and manipulating nested systems

Paradigmatic (14): synthesizes metasystems into new paradigms, exposing the limits of older schemes.

Cross-Paradigmatic (15): weaves disparate paradigms into entirely new interdisciplinary fields (evo-devo marries evolutionary and developmental biology).

Meta-Cross-Paradigmatic (16): reflects recursively on how cross-paradigmatic creations arise and where they fail, modelling the dynamics of transformative thought itself.

Because each order reorganizes the lower ones in a mathematically definable way, progression is quantal (no fuzzy overlaps) and can be scored across cultures, species, or machines by analyzing task structure. Most adults cluster around Abstract or Formal reasoning; systems thinking (12) and the rarer post-formal orders (13-16) typically require sustained education, cross-domain challenges, and environments that reward integrative creativity.
